{"id": "14:34/q21", "question": "What principles of expression and interpretation are discussed in material attached to the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q21/p1", "position": "Subtle language requires thought beyond general vocabulary knowledge or memorization.", "reasons": "Jurjani analyzes a couplet's ordered comparison of distant high moon and emphatic nearness, the words أفرط, شاسع and جد قريب, and quotes the camel saying and Ibn al-Rumi's satire of an unappreciated poet."}, {"id": "14:34/q21/p2", "position": "An exegete begins with clear surface meaning, then may draw context-supported implications and relevant elaborations.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur permits legal and ethical deductions, and astronomy or sound science when they clarify Qur'anic aims; he cites Moses and al-Khidr, creation, economic distribution, mutual interference against multiple gods, moving mountains and a darkened sun."}, {"id": "14:34/q21/p3", "position": "A Quranic encounter with divine generosity may produce love, remembrance and desire for nearness.", "reasons": "Itqan says perceiving a majestic and merciful Lord makes hearts prefer His approval."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q22", "question": "What unrelated report is present in the source material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q22/p1", "position": "Umm Salama reports rules for a pilgrim leaving ihram after stoning and before tawaf.", "reasons": "The Abu Dawud excerpt gives no grading or link to this verse."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q23", "question": "Why are gratitude and disbelief expressed in different tenses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q23/p1", "position": "Recurring gratitude is expressed in the present; disbelief in the past signals it should not recur.", "reasons": "Samarrai states this contrast."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q01", "question": "What governs the opening “when”?", "turns_on": "Whether the earlier clause supplies a suitable governing word and whether the two events must be simultaneous.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q01/p1", "position": "An omitted command, “remember,” governs it.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Razi exclude attachment to the preceding question because the Prophet's time and the youths' retreat were far apart. Ibn Ashur calls this an explanatory restart; Abu Hayyan, Samin, Bursevi and Alusi also allow the ellipsis."}, {"id": "18:10/q01/p2", "position": "It is governed by the preceding “wonder.”", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin, Bursevi and Alusi give this as a syntactic possibility; Bursevi calls it an adverbial attachment."}, {"id": "18:10/q01/p3", "position": "It attaches to “were” in verse 9.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur treats it as a temporal adverb linking the scene to the preceding clause; Alusi also allows this attachment."}, {"id": "18:10/q01/p4", "position": "It attaches to “did you think” in verse 9.", "reasons": "Alusi argues against this because the Prophet's perception was not simultaneous with their retreat; Wahidi and Razi likewise reject attaching it to the preceding question because of the long interval."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q02", "question": "What does “the youths” designate?", "turns_on": "Whether the form is analyzed as a broken plural or collective, and how strictly youth limits its sense.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q02/p1", "position": "It denotes a small group of young men, the Companions of the Cave.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls it a broken plural of paucity, fitting their few number; Ibn Ashur calls it a small-group plural of fully grown youths; Biqai says youth made them receptive to truth. Alusi identifies them as the Cave companions. Ibn Jawzi reports the usual sense as young men; Bursevi adds vigor and the metaphorical use for rulers even when old, and cites a prophetic preference for 'my young man' over 'my slave,' while Abu Yusuf allows bondage."}, {"id": "18:10/q02/p2", "position": "It is a collective plural of fatā on a nonproductive pattern.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Tabrisi and Ibn Jawzi compare ghulām/ghilma and ṣabī/ṣibya; Ibn Jawzi says the pattern cannot freely form analogues such as 'ravens' or 'wealthy men.' Ibn al-Sarraj, cited by Abu Hayyan, calls it a collective noun; Alusi reports other authorities likewise."}, {"id": "18:10/q02/p3", "position": "Fatā can also mean a fully grown man.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, reported by Ibn Jawzi, cites the verse about believing women; Ibn Ashur describes a fully grown youth."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q03", "question": "Why does the verse repeat “the youths” as a noun?", "turns_on": "Whether the explicit noun chiefly foregrounds youth or respects the order by which they became cave companions.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q03/p1", "position": "It draws attention to their youth and its significance.", "reasons": "Alusi says the explicit noun highlights their youth; Ibn Ashur says their close ages evoke mature courage, sound judgment, steadfastness and defense of truth, while Biqai sees youth as receptive to truth."}, {"id": "18:10/q03/p2", "position": "It avoids calling them owners of the cave before they took refuge there.", "reasons": "Alusi says cave ownership results from their retreat, so a pronoun referring back to the earlier title would presuppose it."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q04", "question": "Who were the youths socially, and how many were there?", "turns_on": "The divergent historical reports give different numbers and social roles; the Quran supplies neither their number nor their lineage.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q04/p1", "position": "They were young Roman nobles or sons of prominent families.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq through Tabari calls them freeborn nobles; Tabari's Ubayd report calls them richly dressed princes, with gold ornaments in Abu Hayyan and Alusi. Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi call them sons of nobles; Baydawi, Bursevi and Study Quran report the same setting. Mujahid says one was still downy-bearded. Ibn Ishaq's narrative gives eight."}, {"id": "18:10/q04/p2", "position": "They were close associates or ministers of the king.", "reasons": "Tabrisi's Ubayd account calls them close associates; Study Quran reports courtiers, and Tabatabai lists ministers advising the king among variant reports."}, {"id": "18:10/q04/p3", "position": "They numbered eight.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas in Tabari names the eldest spokesman Mكسلمينا and seven others; Tabari's king confronts eight, and Ibn Ishaq's account in Baghawi and Thalabi has eight elite youths."}, {"id": "18:10/q04/p4", "position": "They numbered seven, including a shepherd in one account.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's account in Qurtubi has seven young secret worshippers and a shepherd with a dog; Tabatabai lists seven including a shepherd among reports."}, {"id": "18:10/q04/p5", "position": "Reports also call them scholars or bathhouse workers.", "reasons": "Tabatabai lists these alternative social identities; Wahb's bathhouse account concerns a disciple who worked there and converted the youths."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q05", "question": "When and within which faith did the youths live?", "turns_on": "Reports place them before or after Jesus, while the Quran itself omits the date.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q05/p1", "position": "They followed Jesus and lived after him.", "reasons": "Amr in Tabari says they followed Jesus; Ibn Ishaq's account makes them Christian believers under a pagan Roman ruler, as do Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Study Quran. Tabrisi says they followed Jesus after the Gospel community had passed. Tabatabai says most historians date them between Jesus and Muhammad and that Christians preserved the story widely."}, {"id": "18:10/q05/p2", "position": "They entered the cave before Jesus.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says Jesus disclosed their story and they rose between Jesus and Muhammad; Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan preserve the alternative pre-Jesus chronology."}, {"id": "18:10/q05/p3", "position": "The Quran leaves their religious affiliation and date unspecified.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says reports link them to Jesus but the Quran selects only instructive details, with no date or place; Tabatabai says the Quran omits historical particulars that do not serve guidance."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q06", "question": "What persecution led to their flight?", "turns_on": "Reports differ on the ruler's religion and the immediate cause of pursuit.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q06/p1", "position": "An idolatrous ruler demanded worship of idols and threatened believers with death.", "reasons": "Yahya says they feared death for faith. Ibn Ishaq names Deqianus/Decius and describes forced sacrifice, mutilation and believers displayed on city walls; Tabari says informers found their prostration, the king summoned eight, stripped their rank and delayed punishment. Qurtubi and Baydawi report refusal and flight; Tabrisi calls the king Daqiyanus in Ephesus. Names vary Daqyus, Daqliyus and Daqinus; Study Quran notes Decius as a possible source of the name."}, {"id": "18:10/q06/p2", "position": "A Magian or Zoroastrian king imposed his religion.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reports this alternative to an idol-worshiping king, also noted by Study Quran from Christian sources."}, {"id": "18:10/q06/p3", "position": "One youth was accused of a crime and the group fled the ruler's pursuit.", "reasons": "Tabari gives this as a separate reported explanation."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q07", "question": "How did the youths come together and leave for the cave?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted narratives give different occasions, escape devices and sequences.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q07/p1", "position": "The young believers met by chance while leaving an idolatrous festival, tested one another's faith, and fled together.", "reasons": "Ubayd ibn Umayr in Tabari and Ibn Atiyya describes independent faith, cautious pairing and disclosure; Mawardi's Mujahid and Tabrisi describe their chance meeting. Some accounts add a hunting dog and 309 years' sleep. Islahi says recognition of truth made them disregard danger."}, {"id": "18:

Ibn Ishaq says they had already prayed, fasted and given alms under persecution."}, {"id": "18:10/q07/p4", "position": "A disciple of Jesus converted them at a bathhouse, then fled with them after two deaths were blamed on the group.", "reasons": "Wahb's report says the king's son and a woman or prostitute died there; a farmer and dog joined, and the king later sealed the cave."}, {"id": "18:10/q07/p5", "position": "Accounts differ on whether they planned together or met by chance, and whether the ruler knew before they fled.", "reasons": "Tabatabai explicitly records these axes of variation."}, {"id": "18:10/q07/p6", "position": "Tamlikha, named as the leader, proposed taking refuge in the cave.", "reasons": "Suyuti names him as the spokesman who proposed the cave; the same note says he spoke after their awakening."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q08", "question": "What happened after they took shelter in the cave?", "turns_on": "The accounts vary in discovery, sealing and later reopening, while agreeing on extraordinary sleep.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q08/p1", "position": "They worshipped there, obtained food secretly, feared the king's search, and were sealed inside.", "reasons": "Tabari says Yemliha entered town disguised as a poor man, returned with news and a meal, and the youths prostrated and prayed for safety. Amr says the people sealed them and a later Christian king reopened the cave. Study Quran says the king expected hunger and thirst to kill them. Tabari also recounts the king's search and his stated willingness to forgive repentance."}, {"id": "18:10/q08/p2", "position": "They slept for 309 years, later awoke and debated how long they had slept.", "reasons": "Ubayd's Tabari report gives 309 years; Amr says they guessed a day or part of one. Suyuti names Tamlikha as the one who said God knew how long they had stayed after awakening."}, {"id": "18:10/q08/p3", "position": "The people failed to find the cave, and later generations found the youths under a Muslim king.", "reasons": "Ubayd's report in Tabari says the search failed, names and lineage were recorded, and a Muslim ruler succeeded the earlier king."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q09", "question": "What is reported about their dog?", "turns_on": "Whether the dog already belonged to a youth or accompanied a shepherd.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q09/p1", "position": "It was a hunting dog belonging to one youth.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi give this account; Muqatil in Qurtubi specifically assigns it to Maksalmina, the eldest youth and owner of sheep. The dog's reported names vary Himran and Qitmir."}, {"id": "18:10/q09/p2", "position": "It was a shepherd's dog that followed its owner and the youths.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi report a shepherd joining them; Tabatabai's report says the shepherd accepted their faith, while other accounts say only the dog followed. Names vary Himran and Qitmir."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q10", "question": "What are the youths' names, and how were they recorded?", "turns_on": "Transmission of the foreign names is weak, and reports differ on who inscribed the record and where it was kept.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q10/p1", "position": "Reports give foreign names, but their transmission is weak.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi note weak transmission; Tabari's list includes Makselminya or Maksalmina as eldest spokesman, Majseliniya, Tamlikha or Yemliha as the one sent with money, Martus, Kashutunus, Birunus, Dinamus and Yatunus. Spellings vary. Suyuti names Tamlikha as the youths' leader, the one who proposed the cave and later said God knew how long they had stayed."}, {"id": "18:10/q10/p2", "position": "Their identities and story were inscribed on metal tablets.", "reasons": "Tabari says two secret believers Bedros and Ronas placed lead tablets in a sealed copper chest by the cave, hoping later believers would find them. Ibn Atiyya reports lead or copper tablets by two believing judges, hidden at their homes or in a building over the cave; Ubayd's report says people recorded their names and lineage."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q11", "question": "Where was their cave?", "turns_on": "Geographic identifications depend on divergent reports and archaeological signs; none is conclusive in Tabatabai's judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q11/p1", "position": "It was Khayram in Mount Yanjalus or Banjulus near Ephesus.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Baghawi give variant forms of the mountain name; reports in Ibn Ishaq and Study Quran place the youths in Ephesus."}, {"id": "18:10/q11/p2", "position": "Rujayb near Amman best fits the site.", "reasons": "Tabatabai prefers Jordanian archaeological signs and some Muslim reports after centuries of ruin and forgetting; he notes Amman's predecessor Philadelphia was a major Roman city."}, {"id": "18:10/q11/p3", "position": "Other proposed sites include Qasiyun, Petra, Scandinavia and Nakhchivan.", "reasons": "Tabatabai lists them, but argues no proposed cave is identified conclusively; Scandinavian and Caucasian claims conflict with Roman geography."}, {"id": "18:10/q11/p4", "position": "The Quran does not locate the event.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says the place and date are not supplied; Tabatabai says such details are omitted because they do not determine guidance."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q12", "question": "What does “took refuge” mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q12/p1", "position": "They went to the cave, settled there and made it their refuge or dwelling.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Thalabi, Baghawi, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, Bursevi and Ibn Jawzi's report from Zajjaj use going and sheltering; Ibn Ashur says it means settling in a dwelling, comparing maʾwā in 10:8. Wahidi transmits Ibn Abbas's gloss of fleeing to it. Jishumi and Tabrisi explain the root as returning to a refuge."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q13", "question": "Why did they seek the cave, and what does their flight teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q13/p1", "position": "They fled persecution to preserve their faith, making religious flight a model.", "reasons": "Yahya, Tabari, Nahhas, Wahidi, Mawardi's Hasan, Tabrisi, Ibn Kathir and Study Quran say they protected religion from an unbelieving people. Qurtubi says believers may leave family, homeland, wealth and friends, citing 16:41 and 9:20 and the Prophet's Companions; Biqai compares Muhammad and Abu Bakr at Thawr. Study Quran's Aj says they despaired of worldly kindness and sought God alone."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q14", "question": "What form of seclusion does their retreat commend?", "turns_on": "Capacity and social conditions determine which kind of seclusion is apt; a prophetic report values patient mixing.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q14/p1", "position": "Retreat from corruption is commendable, with mountains and caves its strongest form.", "reasons": "Qurtubi calls retreat prophetic and saintly, especially in fitna. He cites a Bukhari report on sheep in mountain heights, reports advising staying home and guarding one's tongue, weeping over sin, flight from peak to peak, and a shepherd whose prayer earns forgiveness. He prefers mountain retreat for those able; a reported year-180 permission for celibacy and mountain retreat also appears."}, {"id": "18:10/q14/p2", "position": "Seclusion can be at home, by the coast or frontier, or within a mosque.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says mountains are named as common retreats, but any separation from people counts. He cites reports calling homes cloisters and Badr veterans who stayed home after Uthman's killing; scholars allow coastal and frontier posts, and a prophetic counsel advises staying home."}, {"id": "18:10/q14/p3", "position": "One may remain among people while withdrawing from evil or keeping inward distance.", "reasons": "A group of scholars defines this as inward and practical separation; Ibn al-Mubarak joins remembrance and keeps silent otherwise. Wahb counsels a recluse that people need one another. Qurtubi says some can mix outwardly while distinct inwardly."}, {"id": "18:10/q14/p4", "position": "Patiently mixing with people can be better than avoiding them.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports the Prophet's comparison of a believer who bears people's harm with one who does not mix or bear it."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q15", "question": "What does the cave signify in inward readings?", "turns_on": "Inward interpreters map the physical cave to different dimensions of spiritual refuge.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q15/p1", "position": "It is outward shelter and inward divine care.", "reasons": "Qushayri says God took charge of the youths and brought spiritual states upon them while they were absent from themselves; Study Quran's Aj says they sought God's protection after despairing of the world."}, {"id": "18:10/q15/p2", "position": "It symbolizes the body, where souls develop toward intellectual and practical perfection.", "reasons": "Qashani reads the youths' descent into bodily existence, attachment and tools as a path toward God."}, {"id": "18:10/q15/p3", "position": "It symbolizes the heart.", "reasons": "Study Quran states this mystical reading."}, {"id": "18:10/q15/p4", "position": "It symbolizes solitary encounter with God and escape from the

self.", "reasons": "Bursevi's cited Taʾwilat Najmiyya contrasts their flight from Daqyanus with seekers' flight from existence's darkness to divine beauty and majesty; Alusi reports spiritual chivalry as abandoning everything besides God and ascending through blissful stations."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q16", "question": "What does the “so” before their prayer convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q16/p1", "position": "They prayed immediately on reaching the cave.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reads the fāʾ as indicating haste."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q17", "question": "What mercy did they request?", "turns_on": "Whether mercy names one concrete need or an inclusive gift, and whether it is outward safety, religious aid or inward remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q17/p1", "position": "They sought God's broad help, including forgiveness, provision, protection, guidance, patience or knowledge.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Wahidi give forgiveness and provision; Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi and Study Quran add safety from enemies; Razi adds guidance, knowledge and patience. Alusi prefers an encompassing sense beyond these glosses. Ibn Ashur calls it abundant good in both worlds; Biqai calls it exceptional mercy and al-Harali's highest hidden order. Tabatabai gives divine support or God's exclusive gifts, especially guidance, citing 2:201, 3:194 and 3:8."}, {"id": "18:10/q17/p2", "position": "They asked for provision.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Suddi, Ibn Jawzi, Ibn Atiyya and exegetes cited by Abu Hayyan give this concise gloss; Baghawi reports it as an alternative to guidance in religion. Damghani classifies this request as a case of raḥma meaning provision, alongside 17:28, 35:2 and 18:16; Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha also gives provision and groups 18:16 with it."}, {"id": "18:10/q17/p3", "position": "They asked for guidance in religion.", "reasons": "Baghawi gives this alternative; Tabatabai calls special guidance a gift reserved to God."}, {"id": "18:10/q17/p4", "position": "They asked to be preserved through remembrance and gratitude.", "reasons": "Tustari says preservation in God's remembrance; Sahl in Sulami adds gratitude in every state; Study Quran transmits the remembrance gloss."}, {"id": "18:10/q17/p5", "position": "They asked for rescue from persecution.", "reasons": "Nahhas says rescue from unbelievers; Thalabi says lifting persecution, Tabrisi rescue, Ibn Kathir concealment from their people, and Ibn Ashur protection from exile's hardship and humiliation."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q18", "question": "What does “from Your presence” add?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is a simple source marker or suggests special, unowed divine favor.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q18/p1", "position": "It asks for mercy directly from God's own stores and special bounty.", "reasons": "Yahya's Suddi glosses it as God's presence; Ibn Abbas in Wahidi says this makes them independent of others. Razi says it magnifies the gift fitting divine generosity; Bursevi imagines hidden treasuries beyond hostile sight; Ibn Ashur distinguishes special abundant mercy from universal mercy; Study Quran transmits the storehouse gloss. Abu Hayyan transmits Zamakhshari's gloss of this mercy as forgiveness, provision and safety from enemies."}, {"id": "18:10/q18/p2", "position": "It emphasizes that mercy is a gratuitous favor, not something owed.", "reasons": "Alusi draws this theological implication from the phrase; Tabatabai sees desperate recourse after every other means failed."}, {"id": "18:10/q18/p3", "position": "It simply means “from You.”", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi gives the direct gloss; al-Suddi likewise says 'from God's presence.'"}]}
{"id": "18:10/q19", "question": "Does their prayer seek worldly good, afterlife good, or both?", "turns_on": "The scope of mercy and the relation between the prayer's two clauses.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q19/p1", "position": "It chiefly concerns their worldly predicament.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says they trusted their afterlife outcome, though mercy might include it; Abu Hayyan reports his view and Alusi reports it while rejecting the restriction. Tabatabai identifies the peril after flight from coercion and death."}, {"id": "18:10/q19/p2", "position": "It asks for good in both worlds.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya allows afterlife mercy; Alusi rejects restricting it to worldly affairs; Ibn Ashur calls it comprehensive good in both worlds, and Biqai asks deliverance and guidance in both."}, {"id": "18:10/q19/p3", "position": "Mercy and guidance may name one gift or two distinct requests.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says if mercy means divine support, the guidance clause explains it; if mercy means a specific divine gift, the clause adds another request."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q20", "question": "What does “prepare” mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q20/p1", "position": "Set right, arrange or make easy the means to the desired result.", "reasons": "Wahidi glosses it as set right or prepare; Baghawi says make easy, Ibn Jawzi set right; Baydawi and Tabatabai define the root as bringing a thing into a formed state; Ibn Ashur says furnishing the means to an outcome. Muqatil uses facilitation."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q21", "question": "How is “prepare” read and explained phonologically?", "turns_on": "Whether hamza is retained, replaced with yāʾ, or removed by a further weak-letter process.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q21/p1", "position": "The common reading retains hamza after the doubled yāʾ.", "reasons": "Samin states this is the majority form; the alternative replaces or deletes the hamza."}, {"id": "18:10/q21/p2", "position": "Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba and al-Zuhri read two yāʾs without hamza.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi say a quiescent hamza is replaced with yāʾ. Qiraat-ER argues the replacement could change the root from h-y-ʾ to h-w-y and shade the sense toward making desirable or inclining."}, {"id": "18:10/q21/p3", "position": "A reading transmitted from ʿAsim lacks hamza by replacement or deletion.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan cites Ibn Khalawayh's al-Aʿsha from Abu Bakr from ʿAsim: replacement is regular, while deletion is disputed but allowed in imperatives and jussives. Samin says the replacement may be treated as an original weak letter and then deleted, citing a poem; Alusi also gives both routes."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q22", "question": "How is the hamza of “prepare” written?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q22/p1", "position": "Here it is seated on alif, though common spelling normally follows the preceding vowel.", "reasons": "Farra says Arabs sometimes use alif in every position and reports the ʿAbd Allah codex spelling شيأ and يستهزأون with alif. The more common book pattern uses vowel-conditioned seats, though the alif pattern reflects the hamza's origin. Al-Ghazi ibn Qays reports alif for the hamza of hayyiʾ and yuhayyiʾ in some codices to avoid excessive deletion after a doubled yāʾ. Al-Sakhawi says al-Dani lacked knowledge of the Syrian codex, and Ibn al-Jazari says he saw those forms there."}, {"id": "18:10/q22/p2", "position": "The hamza is written according to the preceding vowel, with two yāʾ letters in hayyiʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Dani rejects alif as contrary to consensus; al-Shatibi and others specify two yāʾ letters. Suyuti states the vowel-conditioned hamza-seat rule and cites wa-hayyiʾ as its example."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q23", "question": "Why are the prepositional phrases placed before the requested object?", "turns_on": "Whether fronting chiefly highlights the beneficiaries and affair or recasts the whole affair as rightness.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q23/p1", "position": "Their fronting emphasizes the desired favor and brings it into view early.", "reasons": "Muqatil notes fronting; Alusi says it focuses the petition's object from the outset. Bursevi says both phrases attach to 'prepare.'"}, {"id": "18:10/q23/p2", "position": "The construction rhetorically extracts guidance from their affair, meaning make the whole affair right.", "reasons": "Alusi gives this as another rhetorical analysis; Zamakhshari's comparison to calling someone a lion is reported by Abu Hayyan."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q24", "question": "What is “our affair” in the prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun points narrowly to their migration or broadly to every aspect of their situation.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q24/p1", "position": "It is their flight from unbelievers and their effort to remain faithful.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi and Alusi identify separation from unbelievers; Bursevi adds perseverance in obedience. Ibn Ashur includes faith and refuge, for which God prepared concealment, bodily preservation, long sleep and their later public sign. Tabatabai describes their peril after persecutors killed or coerced believers."}, {"id": "18:10/q24/p2", "position": "It is their entire situation or all their affairs.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi and Nasafi allow the whole affair to be ordered; Razi and Abu Hayyan report making the affair itself guided, with a simile to calling someone a lion."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q25", "question": "What is the right course they ask God to prepare?", "turns_on": "Whether right guidance refers chiefly to religious conduct, safe escape, sound judgment, facilitation, or the character of the whole affair.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q25/p1", "position": "Guidance to conduct pleasing to God, nearness to Him and steadfast faith.", "reasons": "Tabari links ease in what pleases God, escape from idolatry and sound action, citing 4:6; Zajjaj, Wahidi's Abu Ishaq, Ibn Jawzi, Baghawi, Thalabi, Tabrisi and Nasafi speak of nearness and pleasure.  says a safe exit from the cave. {"id": "18:10/q26", "question": "How is “right guidance” read here?", "turns_on": "Both forms convey guidance, but the common form matches the surrounding cadence and has a different usage profile.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q26/p1", "position": "The common reading is rashadan, with fatḥa on both consonants.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Nahhas, Ibn Atiyya, Samin and Alusi say it matches the verse endings; Abu Hayyan reports Ibn Atiyya's preference. Ibn al-Jazari reports unanimous opening of rāʾ and shīn in 18:10 and 18:24 and favors the cadence with nearby endings ʿajaban, ʿadadan and aḥadan (18:9, 18:12, 18:49). Suyuti says choosing between permissible vocal forms can serve the sura's cadence and rejects al-Farisi's preference for the other form."}, {"id": "18:10/q26/p2", "position": "Abu Raja reads rushdan, with ḍamma on rāʾ and still shīn.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi report it; Alusi says its meaning is the same. {"id": "18:10/q27", "question": "What does their prayer teach about dependence on God?", "turns_on": "The notes draw complementary lessons from the appeal rather than dispute its wording.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q27/p1", "position": "It models helpless, sincere recourse to God and a request for a good outcome.", "reasons": "Qushayri says they disavow their own power and receive divine care; Tabatabai sees exhausted means; Ibn Kathir cites a transmitted prayer for every decree to end well, and a report from Busr says the Prophet sought good ends and protection from worldly disgrace and afterlife punishment. Study Quran compares the same hadith; Qurtubi says the Prophet prayed when troubled. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan recommend this verse as sufficient for believers' worldly needs; Islahi calls their request wise."}, {"id": "18:10/q27/p2", "position": "Their prayer expresses God's lordship and refusal to invoke another deity.", "reasons": "Thalabi connects it with their declaration that God alone is Lord of heaven and earth and that another invocation would be an outrageous falsehood."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q28", "question": "How do inward readers understand the youths' state and request?", "turns_on": "Different inward readings map the story to divine witnessing, embodied development or remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q28/p1", "position": "They receive divine care and pass through loss of self-awareness into sober witnessing.", "reasons": "Qushayri says God shelters them inwardly, effaces their self-awareness in unity and self-sufficiency, then returns them to discrimination; their prayer relinquishes reliance on their own power."}, {"id": "18:10/q28/p2", "position": "Their request seeks the beautiful names, spiritual development and perfection through bodily life.", "reasons": "Qashani reads mercy as gifts fitting their readiness, and guidance as intellectual and practical perfection along a steady course toward God."}, {"id": "18:10/q28/p3", "position": "Their continued life can symbolize remembrance beyond ordinary time.", "reasons": "Study Quran relates this to the inward sense of divine remembrance during their prolonged sleep."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q29", "question": "What explains the awe and flight associated with seeing the youths later in the story?", "turns_on": "Whether emphasis falls on the divine awe manifested in them or the observer's standpoint.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q29/p1", "position": "Divine light, majesty and overpowering spiritual states in them cause the onlooker to flee.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata in Sulami says lights of the Real surround them; Husayn points to their states despite their nearness; Jafar calls the awe God's power, care and guardianship. Another voice distinguishes angelic honoring lights from human outward and inward guidance, comparing Satan fleeing Umar."}, {"id": "18:10/q29/p2", "position": "Flight follows seeing them from the human self; seeing from God yields unity and firmness.", "reasons": "Jafar contrasts human and divine perspectives and compares the Prophet's flight from unbelievers; Ibn Ata says the Prophet beholds God and is beheld from Him, so merely created sight turns away."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q30", "question": "How does this verse connect to the surrounding account?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the entry prayer to the story's structure, later speech, and the Moses narrative.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q30/p1", "position": "It opens a short summary of their flight, prayer, sleep and awakening before the fuller story.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the outline shows their protection as support for faith and that the episode is not God's most astonishing sign. Tabatabai identifies three summary elements, then later discovery and mosque; Islahi says this Quranic narrative pattern protects the main lesson from incidental details. Asad says the prayer previews verse 13 onward."}, {"id": "18:10/q30/p2", "position": "Their later confidence that God will grant mercy and ease recalls this entry prayer.", "reasons": "Tabatabai links their advice after leaving the people and gods with the gifts first requested on entering the cave. Damghani and Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha group the prayer's mercy with the mercy mentioned later at 18:16, glossing it as provision."}, {"id": "18:10/q30/p3", "position": "The certainty of the promise of mercy and provision in verse 16 marks it as God's speech.", "reasons": "Islahi rejects exegetes who attribute that promise to the youths: a humble speaker could express it only as prayer or yearning, as in verse 10."}, {"id": "18:10/q30/p4", "position": "Khiḍr's mercy and knowledge and Moses' sound judgment echo the youths' two requests.", "reasons": "Study Quran compares the gift to Khidr at 18:60 and Moses' request for sound judgment with the cave youths' prayer."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q31", "question": "Why was the Cave story related to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q31/p1", "position": "Quraysh tested him with questions obtained from Jewish scholars.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan names al-Nadr and Uqba and questions about the youths, a world traveler and the spirit; another report says answering two while withholding one would confirm prophethood. {"id": "18:10/q32", "question": "What larger themes does the account serve?", "turns_on": "The story bears on resurrection, faith under persecution and the sura's presentation of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q32/p1", "position": "It demonstrates resurrection and the coming Hour.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says long sleep and awakening make these ideas easier to grasp; the townspeople's recognition is part of the instructive narrative."}, {"id": "18:10/q32/p2", "position": "It supports faith and places this sign within the sura's larger praise of revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says protection supports their faith; Abu Hayyan links this sura's praise of the upright warning Quran, its warning against claims of a divine son and its promise to believers, with the preceding sura's truth of revelation and humility at 17:105."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q33", "question": "How should the many historical reports about the cave be treated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q33/p1", "position": "Their particulars diverge, while the Quran selects the details needed for guidance.", "reasons": "Tabatabai lists disagreements on rulers, date, number, dog, names and titles; he attributes them to widespread Christian and Jewish storytelling and Muslim collection of outside reports via converts such as Wahb and Ka'b, later elevated to prophetic reports. {"id": "18:10/q37", "question": "What is the status of the report about reciting Surat al-Kahf?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q37/p1", "position": "A report promises light for reciting its beginning and end, and greater light for the whole sura.", "reasons": "Thalabi transmits it from Muadh as a saying of the Prophet: head-to-foot light for the ends and earth-to-heaven light for the whole."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q38", "question": "How does Sibawayh parse the similar form fatīya in a war poem and its grammatical parallels?", "turns_on": "The reported parses differ on whether the poem's fatīya is a nominative predicate or an accusative state.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q38/p1", "position": "In the cited war poem, fatīya can be nominative: war's first stage is a maiden.", "reasons": "Sibawayh reports a parse taking the first stage as a maiden, with feminine agreement as in 'some of his fingers went.' His examples make accusatives states understood with idh kāna or idhā kāna; comparisons, attributed day and night states, and the necessarily accusative qāʾiman illustrate this. {"id": "18:10/q39", "question": "What is the lexical sense of mercy in their request?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q39/p1", "position": "Mercy is a blessing granted to one in need, with a root sense of tenderness.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha defines it as a blessing for someone in need and reports Ibn Fāris's connection of raḥima, raḥm, marḥama and raḥma with tenderness."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q40", "question": "How does grammatical attachment affect the suitability of a pause in this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q40/p1", "position": "A pause is less suitable where a dependent is more tightly attached to its governing word.", "reasons": "Burhan states this as a general principle for judging pauses by the strength of grammatical attachment."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q41", "question": "How can the past-tense refuge narrative and the ensuing prayer be coordinated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q41/p1", "position": "They can be coordinated as clauses; the narrow rule for syntactic verb-to-verb following applies only to imperfect verbs in subjunctive or jussive form.", "reasons": "Burhan reports the author of al-Mustawfa's narrow rule, then answers the objection from past-tense narrative followed by prayer by distinguishing clause coordination from inflectional following of verbs that share case or mood."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q42", "question": "What is reported about pausing on the hamza of 'prepare'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q42/p1", "position": "Full articulation of this hamza at a pause and deletion of the substituted long-vowel letter for jussive syntax are rejected.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari applies the preceding rule to hayyiʾ and yuhayyiʾ, along with nabbiʾ, iqraʾ and nashaʾ, and rejects both proposed treatments."}]}
{"id": "18:10/q43", "question": "How is the related expression min ladunhu elsewhere in the sura vocalized?", "turns_on": "The reports distinguish vowels and connecting letters in a related ladun expression.", "positions": [{"id": "18:10/q43/p1", "position": "Abu Bakr gives the dāl sukūn with a hint of ḍamma, kasra on the nūn and hāʾ, and a connecting yāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari reports Abu Bakr's detailed vocalization of the related form."}, {"id": "18:10/q43/p2", "position": "In a route from Abu Bakr, the hāʾ has kasra without a connecting vowel.", "reasons": "Nafṭawayh transmits this route through al-Ṣarīfīnī and Yaḥyā, as does Khalaf from Yaḥyā."}, {"id": "18:10/q43/p3", "position": "The remaining readers give the dāl and hāʾ ḍamma and leave the nūn unvocalized; Ibn Kathir connects the hāʾ with wāw.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari reports the majority vocalization and Ibn Kathir's regular connecting wāw."}]}
{"id": "18:103/q01", "question": "What does the command قُلْ signal, and who carries it out?", "turns_on": "Whether the command is understood as the Prophet's delivery alone or as also involving believers.", "positions": [{"id": "18:103/q01/p1", "position": "Muhammad is commanded to deliver an important warning to the heedless and unbelievers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says opening with 'say' marks an utterance worthy of attention; Biqāʿī describes recipients whose eyes and ears fail to heed remembrance."}, {"id": "18:103/q01/p2", "position": "The Prophet and the believers who follow him announce the warning.", "reasons": "Bursevī extends the command's delivery to believers alongside the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "18:103/q02", "question": "What force does هَلْ have in this question?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish an inviting offer, rebuke, ironic offer, and several reported uses of hal.", "positions": [{"id": "18:103/q02/p1", "position": "It is an inviting prompt meaning 'shall we' or 'would you like us to'.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī's lexicon applies the 'alā' use to 18:103 and compares 20:10, 26:221, 34:7, and 61:10."}, {"id": "18:103/q02/p2", "position": "It is a rebuking or emphatic question.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba likens hal to the interrogative hamza, citing 27:60; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this question a taunting rebuke of unbelievers."}, {"id": "18:103/q02/p3", "position": "It offers to inform the hearers ironically, since the disclosure does not depend on their assent.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the speaker will inform them regardless; Ālūsī calls the supposed request for leave deeply sarcastic."}, {"id": "18:103/q02/p4", "position": "In ordinary use, it can be a genuine question.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī's lexicon illustrates this with 7:53, 10:35, 30:28, and 50:30; it does not explicitly select this use for 18:103."}, {"id": "18:103/q02/p5", "position": "It can mean qad, introducing a report.", "reasons": "The lexicon cites questions introducing Moses, the disputants, Abraham's guests, the human being, and the Overwhelming Event: 20:9, 38:21, 51:24, 76:1, 88:1."}, {"id": "18:103/q02/p6", "position": "It can mean mā, with a negative or exclusive implied answer.", "reasons": "The lexicon compares 2:210, 6:158, 7:53, 16:35, 43:66, and 55:60."}, {"id": "18:103/q02/p7", "position": "It is said to mean illā here.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān lists 18:103 as an example of this usage."}]}
{"id": "18:103/q03", "question": "Who is meant by the plural speaker in نُنَبِّئُكُم?", "turns_on": "The nūn may be divine majesty, a shared speaker, or a signal about prior knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "18:103/q03/p1", "position": "It is God's majestic plural, with a shift from the expected third-person 'He informs you'.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this explanation of the plural nūn."}, {"id": "18:103/q03/p2", "position": "It refers to God together with the Messenger.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this as one alternative."}, {"id": "18:103/q03/p3", "position": "It refers to the Messenger together with the Muslims.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this as the other alternative; Bursevī includes believers among those told to deliver the announcement."}, {"id": "18:103/q03/p4", "position": "The plural either identifies the speaker at once or intimates that believers already know the news.", "reasons": "Ālūsī gives both rhetorical explanations."}]}
{"id": "18:103/q04", "question": "To whom is the address كُم directed?", "turns_on": "The notes specify the audience at different levels: unbelievers, contextual polytheists, and the heedless.", "positions": [{"id": "18:103/q04/p1", "position": "It addresses unbelievers, particularly the polytheists in the surrounding passage.", "reasons": "Bursevī names unbelievers; Ālūsī says the question addresses unbelievers; Ibn ʿĀshūr says polytheists are rebuked and alerted to their failed efforts; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says their identity is confirmed by the later denial of God's signs and meeting."}, {"id": "18:103/q04/p2", "position": "It warns people heedless of remembrance, whose eyes and ears miss the warning.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī takes the addressees from the preceding description."}]}

 "position": "The question rebukes the hearers and builds curiosity before exposing them as the losers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it a taunting rebuke; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the shift from second to third person delays the reveal that the listeners themselves are meant, and calls the offer ironic; Ālūsī notes its sarcasm."}]}
{"id": "18:103/q06", "question": "Who are the greatest losers in deeds?", "turns_on": "The disagreement concerns whether named communities are exclusive referents, illustrative cases, or displaced by the immediate polytheist context; reports from ʿAlī and Saʿd differ.", "positions": [{"id": "18:103/q06/p1", "position": "They are Jews and Christians, or the disbelieving People of the Book.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī cites 88:3–4; Saʿd says Jews denied Muhammad and Christians denied food and drink in Paradise, while calling the Kharijites covenant breakers; Biqāʿī adds that both deny bodily resurrection. Al-ʿAyyāshī's report describes scriptural communities that disbelieved and innovated. Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya treat specific reports as applications, not the original referent."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p2", "position": "They are monks and priests, especially Christian ascetics confined in cells or monasteries.", "reasons": "ʿAlī is repeatedly cited; al-Ḍaḥḥāk also appears. Abū Ḥayyān compares the 'toiling, weary' language of 88:3. Reports vary between cells, monasteries, and pillars; Jishumī gives this as an occasion of revelation. Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects its status as the original contextual referent."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p3", "position": "They are the polytheists who worship idols or other beings and think that worship benefits them.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī says the question rebukes those worshipping other than God; Ibn ʿĀshūr connects it to reliance on useless idol patrons; Ṭabāṭabāʾī appeals to 18:106 and the surrounding passage. Biqāʿī lists angels, stars, prophets, idols, and other unbelief; Kur'an Yolu says idolaters deem shirk obedience. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the next verse fits Meccan idolaters."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p4", "position": "They include the Harurites or Kharijites.", "reasons": "Reports attribute this to ʿAlī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Abū ʿAlī; one al-ʿAyyāshī report says they are 'not far' from the People of the Book. Jishumī would accept ʿAlī's report if authentic, arguing that kufr can include rejection of some signs. Al-Aṣamm objects that the verse describes unbelievers while the Harurites are Muslims; Saʿd explicitly names another group. Ibn Kathīr calls them included but not exclusive; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the Jewish-to-Kharijite report unsound."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p5", "position": "The label broadly covers anyone whose unapproved religious path seems sound to its follower.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says named groups are examples rather than an exhaustive definition, including outsiders to Islam, show-offs, and heretics whose innovations reach unbelief. Ibn Kathīr says the Meccan date precedes Kharijites and the relevant Jewish-Christian address, and cites 88:2–4, 25:23, and 24:39. He says these people believe their deeds accepted and beloved."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p6", "position": "They are the sinful or transgressive people of Quraysh.", "reasons": "Two reports attribute this answer to ʿAlī when Ibn al-Kawwāʾ asked him; the second cites 18:103–104."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p7", "position": "They are adherents of religious whims or heresies.", "reasons": "Māwardī records the first description; Abū Ḥayyān includes innovators whose heresy leads to unbelief within the broad warning."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p8", "position": "They are show-offs or people who boast of good deeds.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports boasters; Abū Ḥayyān includes show-offs as an application."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p9", "position": "They are hypocrites whose deeds contradict belief.", "reasons": "Māwardī records this possible referent."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p10", "position": "They are people who seek this world and abandon the next.", "reasons": "Māwardī gives this possibility twice, once alongside hypocrites."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p11", "position": "They are the Sabians.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān records this among the named groups."}, {"id": "18:103/q06/p12", "position": "They are Christians specifically.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes a report naming Christians without a wider group."}]}
{"id": "18:103/q07", "question": "What degree or kind of loss does ٱلْأَخْسَرِينَ express?", "turns_on": "Whether the explanation stresses the comparative degree or the practical image of fruitless investment.", "positions": [{"id": "18:103/q07/p1", "position": "It marks the greatest or more severe loss among losers or among creation.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī says akhsar exceeds khāsir and ranks some losers below others; Wāḥidī says these deeds make them the greatest losers among creation; Bursevī similarly says greatest loss among creatures."}, {"id": "18:103/q07/p2", "position": "It portrays exhausting effort that ends in ruin, like a merchant who expects profit but loses the investment.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī and Baghawī use the failed merchant analogy; Wāḥidī al-Wajīz says their deeds are disastrously lost."}]}
{"id": "18:103/q08", "question": "How is أَعْمَٰلًا parsed, and why is it plural?", "turns_on": "The main analysis takes aʿmālan as tamyīz; alternatives differ over its underlying singular and whether it denotes workers.", "positions": [{"id": "18:103/q08/p1", "position": "It is an accusative specification of the loss; its plural reflects diverse deeds, desires, or agents.", "reasons": "Sībawayh notes that the definite plural adjective retains nūn, preventing annexation; al-Akhfash likewise says the article and plural ending require accusative specification.
